meta.title: Bank Lending & Credit Management
meta.description: This 9 Module course is designed to enable participants demonstrate understanding of the techniques of a good credit assessment, with particular emphasis on evaluating the risks associated to lending. The course covers analysis of accounting statements for lending purposes; assessment of a lending proposition; factors creating credit risks and its control; security; lending requirements of different types of business; advances; other specialist bank services related to lending.

modules.title: Practical Application of Financial Statements to Lending Decisions

questionBank.q: In everyday banking usage, which of the following best captures the basic meaning of the word 'credit'?
opts: Being granted permanent forgiveness of a repayment obligation
Being permitted to receive goods or services now and pay for them later
Being assigned a fixed monthly allowance by a lender
Being required to pay for goods or services before receiving them
questionBank.ans: Being permitted to receive goods or services now and pay for them later
questionBank.exp: Credit is the permission to delay payment for goods or services already received. (A) reverses the timing, (C) confuses credit with debt forgiveness, and (D) confuses it with a budgeted allowance rather than a repayment arrangement.

questionBank.q: A borrower signs an agreement receiving funds today in exchange for a promise to repay later, generally with interest. Which of the three practical meanings of 'credit' does this illustrate?
questionBank.exp: This describes Credit as a Contractual Obligation — an agreement to repay with interest. Borrowing Capacity is the amount available to draw, Accounting Term is a ledger entry, and Credit Risk is a different concept (likelihood of default) rather than one of the three meanings.

questionBank.q: Which of the three practical meanings of 'credit' refers to the amount of money an entity is able to draw down because it must eventually be repaid to the lender?
questionBank.exp: Borrowing Capacity is the amount available to be borrowed. Contractual Obligation and Accounting Term are the other two meanings, and Collateral is a different concept entirely (an asset pledged as security).

questionBank.q: On a company's statement of financial position, recording a credit entry has which effect?
opts: It decreases an asset or increases a liability or equity account
It always increases net income regardless of which account is affected
It decreases a liability or increases an asset account
It decreases both assets and liabilities simultaneously
questionBank.ans: It decreases an asset or increases a liability or equity account
questionBank.exp: As an accounting term, a credit either decreases assets or increases liabilities and equity. (A) reverses the mechanic, (C) misapplies the income-statement effect to every account, and (D) describes a mechanic not supported by the material.

questionBank.q: A relationship officer updates a customer's file in a way that increases the recorded balance of a liability account on the bank's books, with no cash exchanged and no new promise made to the customer. Which of the three meanings of 'credit' best applies to what has just happened?
questionBank.exp: An entry that increases a liability account without any new agreement or cash movement is the Accounting Term sense of credit. Contractual Obligation would require a new promise, Borrowing Capacity concerns an available amount, and Credit Risk is unrelated.

questionBank.q: How is credit risk defined?
opts: The likelihood that a borrower will fail to repay the principal and interest owed when due
The certainty that a borrower will default within the facility's first year
The likelihood that a borrower's collateral will lose market value
The likelihood that a bank will run short of liquid deposits
questionBank.ans: The likelihood that a borrower will fail to repay the principal and interest owed when due
questionBank.exp: Credit risk is the likelihood that a borrower will be unable to repay principal and interest when due. (A) describes liquidity risk, (C) describes a collateral/market-value concern, and (D) overstates risk as certainty with a timeframe the definition does not include.

questionBank.q: When a bank extends a lending facility, what two things does it expect from the borrower?
opts: Full principal repayment at any time before maturity and waiver of interest
Timely repayment of the principal sum and timely payment of interest
Timely repayment of the principal sum and provision of additional collateral
Timely payment of interest only, since principal is expected at final maturity
questionBank.ans: Timely repayment of the principal sum and timely payment of interest
questionBank.exp: A bank expects timely repayment of principal and timely payment of interest. (A) substitutes collateral for interest, (C) and (D) each drop one of the two genuine expectations.

questionBank.q: A bank increases lending across several sectors partly because it sees this as central to its role in the wider economy. A separate lending decision at another bank is driven mainly by the fact that lending is its single largest source of income. Which reasons for bank lending do these two decisions respectively illustrate?
opts: National Economic Growth & Investment, then Profit Generation
National Economic Growth & Investment, then Regulatory Requirements
Profit Generation, then National Economic Growth & Investment
questionBank.ans: National Economic Growth & Investment, then Profit Generation
questionBank.exp: The first bank is acting on National Economic Growth & Investment (lending to promote growth across sectors); the second is acting on Profit Generation (lending as the largest income source). The other options mismatch or reverse the pairing.

questionBank.q: A bank's capital and liquidity adequacy requirements would trigger sanctions if it failed to maintain a certain level of lending. Which reason for bank lending does this scenario illustrate?
questionBank.exp: Sanctions tied to capital and liquidity adequacy requirements point to Regulatory Requirements as the reason for lending. The other three are genuine reasons for bank lending but do not involve sanctions for non-adherence.

questionBank.q: A bank funds new loans from customer deposits while keeping enough liquid assets on hand to meet withdrawal demand. Which reason for bank lending is being demonstrated?
questionBank.exp: Using deposits to lend while preserving enough liquid assets to meet customer demand is Liquidity Management. The other options describe different reasons for lending not centered on balancing deposits against withdrawal demand.

questionBank.q: A bank is sanctioned by its regulator for falling short of a mandated lending threshold. A different bank, in a separate case, restricts new lending because it fears it cannot meet upcoming customer withdrawals. Which reasons for bank lending do these two situations respectively illustrate?
opts: Profit Generation, then National Economic Growth & Investment
questionBank.exp: The first case involves sanctions for missing a lending threshold — Regulatory Requirements. The second involves preserving capacity to meet withdrawals — Liquidity Management. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: In the credit thought process, what is the first step a credit analyst carries out?
opts: Conducting financial analysis of the borrower
questionBank.exp: The sequence begins with Identification of the Borrower, before information is gathered or analysis is performed. The other options are later steps in the same process.

questionBank.q: During which step of the credit thought process does the analyst collect details about a borrower's character and capacity?
questionBank.exp: Gathering Information is the step where character and capacity details are collated. The other steps involve identifying the borrower, examining financial statements, and assessing the business environment respectively.

questionBank.q: An analyst reviewing a corporate customer's financial statements calculates several ratios to judge financial health before recommending a facility. Which step of the credit thought process is being performed?
questionBank.exp: Calculating ratios to assess financial health is Financial Analysis. The other steps involve collecting borrower information, identifying the borrower, and examining the business environment respectively.

questionBank.q: Before recommending a facility to a textile manufacturer, an analyst studies how import tariffs and competitor pricing could affect the customer's ability to repay. Which step of the credit thought process is this?
questionBank.exp: Studying tariffs and competitor pricing is Industry & Market Analysis. The other steps involve financial statement analysis, general information collection, and identifying the borrower respectively.

questionBank.q: Placed in the correct order, which sequence reflects how the credit thought process actually proceeds?
opts: Identification of Borrower, Financial Analysis, Gathering Information, Industry & Market Analysis
Gathering Information, Identification of Borrower, Industry & Market Analysis, Financial Analysis
Financial Analysis, Gathering Information, Identification of Borrower, Industry & Market Analysis
Identification of Borrower, Gathering Information, Financial Analysis, Industry & Market Analysis
questionBank.ans: Identification of Borrower, Gathering Information, Financial Analysis, Industry & Market Analysis
questionBank.exp: The correct sequence is Identification of Borrower, Gathering Information, Financial Analysis, then Industry & Market Analysis. The other options reorder these steps out of sequence.

questionBank.q: Application submission and data gathering both occur at one stage of the credit process, while contract preparation and legal-instrument drafting occur at a later stage. Which two stages does this describe, in order?
opts: Credit Marketing, then Credit Decision Making
Credit Analysis, then Credit Decision Making
questionBank.exp: Application submission and data gathering belong to Credit Marketing; contract and legal-instrument preparation belong to Legal & Documentation, which occurs later in the sequence. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: A credit officer reviews a prospective borrower's financial stability and assesses the risks attached to the proposal, before any decision is made on the facility. Which stage of the credit process is this?
questionBank.exp: Reviewing financial stability and assessing risk, ahead of any decision, is Credit Analysis. The other stages involve marketing the facility, deciding on it, and documenting it legally, respectively.

questionBank.q: A credit committee weighs whether to approve a facility and, if so, how it should be structured. Which stage of the credit process does this represent?
questionBank.exp: Weighing approval and structure is Credit Decision Making. Credit Analysis precedes this decision, Credit Approval & Disbursement follows it, and Credit Marketing is earlier still.

questionBank.q: Funds are released into a customer's account after every required document has been signed and internal sign-off has been obtained. Which stage of the credit process has just occurred?
questionBank.exp: Releasing funds after documentation and sign-off is Credit Approval & Disbursement. The other stages occur earlier in the process, before funds are released.

questionBank.q: After disbursement, an account officer periodically reviews a loan, reports on its performance, and stays in contact with the borrower to catch early signs of default. Which stage of the credit process covers this?
questionBank.exp: Ongoing review, reporting, and communication after disbursement fall under Credit Monitoring & Management. Approval & Disbursement and Analysis occur earlier, and Collection is a distinct, later stage.

questionBank.q: Loan termination and post-loan analysis both belong to which stage of the credit process?
questionBank.exp: Loan termination and post-loan analysis are both activities within Credit Collection, the final stage. The other stages involve ongoing monitoring, disbursement, and legal documentation respectively.

questionBank.q: A relationship manager keeps in regular contact with a struggling borrower and begins recovery efforts while the facility is still active. In a separate file, a different loan has already been fully closed out and the officer is now conducting a post-loan review. Which stages of the credit process do these two activities respectively belong to?
opts: Credit Monitoring & Management, then Credit Collection
Credit Monitoring & Management, then Credit Analysis
Credit Analysis, then Credit Approval & Disbursement
Credit Collection, then Credit Monitoring & Management
questionBank.ans: Credit Monitoring & Management, then Credit Collection
questionBank.exp: Contact and recovery efforts on an active facility fall under Credit Monitoring & Management; the post-loan review on a closed file falls under Credit Collection. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: A loan file shows that the offer letter and board resolution have both been signed, but the bank has not yet released any funds into the customer's account. Which stage of the credit process does this file currently sit between?
opts: Credit Approval & Disbursement and Credit Monitoring & Management
Credit Decision Making and Legal & Documentation
Legal & Documentation and Credit Approval & Disbursement
questionBank.ans: Legal & Documentation and Credit Approval & Disbursement
questionBank.exp: Signed documentation with no funds yet released places the file between Legal & Documentation and Credit Approval & Disbursement. The other pairings describe stages that either precede documentation or assume disbursement has already occurred.

questionBank.q: Which key success factor for a credit analyst is described as a strong understanding of financial statements paired with good analytical skill?
questionBank.exp: Financial Acumen is defined as a strong understanding of financial statements and good analytical skills. The other factors involve evaluating credit risk, documentation accuracy, and regulatory awareness respectively.

questionBank.q: One analyst is recognized for evaluating credit risk effectively, while a colleague is recognized for staying current on laws and compliance requirements that affect lending. Which key success factors are being recognized, respectively?
opts: Credit Risk Assessment Skills, then Regulatory Compliance Awareness
Credit Risk Assessment Skills, then Financial Acumen
Regulatory Compliance Awareness, then Credit Risk Assessment Skills
Financial Acumen, then Attention to Detail
questionBank.ans: Credit Risk Assessment Skills, then Regulatory Compliance Awareness
questionBank.exp: Evaluating credit risk effectively is Credit Risk Assessment Skills; staying current on relevant laws and compliance requirements is Regulatory Compliance Awareness. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: An analyst double-checks a facility's documentation and stated tenor before submission, to avoid inaccuracies that could breach lending policy. Which key success factor is being applied?
questionBank.exp: Checking documentation and tenor for accuracy is Attention to Detail. The other factors involve broader compliance awareness, financial statement skill, and risk evaluation respectively, not line-level accuracy checking.

questionBank.q: An analyst declines to omit a material weakness from a credit report even though doing so would make approval easier, because merit and compliance should guide the recommendation. Which key success factor is being applied?
questionBank.exp: Choosing merit and compliance over an easier but incomplete report reflects Ethical Judgement. The other factors involve documentation accuracy, legal/regulatory awareness, and financial analysis skill respectively.

questionBank.q: One analyst is praised for never missing an inaccurate figure in a loan file, while a colleague is praised for always knowing which new regulations affect a given facility type. Which key success factors are being recognized, respectively?
opts: Attention to Detail, then Financial Acumen
Attention to Detail, then Regulatory Compliance Awareness
Regulatory Compliance Awareness, then Attention to Detail
Financial Acumen, then Credit Risk Assessment Skills
questionBank.ans: Attention to Detail, then Regulatory Compliance Awareness
questionBank.exp: Catching inaccurate figures is Attention to Detail; tracking new regulations affecting facility types is Regulatory Compliance Awareness. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: The profit equation referenced among a credit analyst's other key success factors is expressed as which formula?
questionBank.exp: The stated profit equation is Profit = Revenue minus Cost (P=R-C). The other options substitute Risk or Recovery for Revenue, or reverse the operation.

questionBank.q: Rather than simply approving or declining a facility as requested, an analyst redesigns the repayment schedule and adds a covenant to bring the risk down to an acceptable level. Which other key success factor does this reflect?
opts: Ability to match risk and reward
Ability to propose appropriate credit structure and risk mitigants
questionBank.ans: Ability to propose appropriate credit structure and risk mitigants
questionBank.exp: Redesigning the schedule and adding a covenant is proposing an appropriate credit structure and risk mitigant. The other factors describe understanding the business, focusing on profitability, and weighing risk against reward, none of which is what occurred here.

questionBank.q: A long-standing depositor with no prior lending relationship approaches an officer to fund a poultry-processing venture she has never operated before. Before assessing the numbers, which key success factor should the officer prioritize first?
opts: Ability to match risk and reward
questionBank.exp: Facing an unfamiliar business type, the officer should first prioritize understanding the customer's business before the numbers can be meaningfully assessed. The other factors matter later in the process, once the business itself is understood.

questionBank.q: A fuel-retail customer has stopped repaying installments on schedule, and the facility is still active on the bank's books. The relationship officer follows up directly with the customer and reviews the account regularly to look for a path back to performance. Which stage of the credit process is the officer currently carrying out?
questionBank.exp: Regular follow-up and account review on a still-active facility is Credit Monitoring & Management, which includes potential-default response. Credit Collection applies once the loan has been terminated, and Analysis and Decision Making occur earlier.

questionBank.q: According to the passage on why credit analysis matters, how does the bank treat officers who fail its Credit Policy guidelines test, compared to how it treats officers who consistently get lending decisions right?
opts: The former are penalised, while the latter are rewarded with rapid promotion
The former are penalised, while the latter receive no special recognition
The former are rewarded with rapid promotion, while the latter are penalised
Both are treated the same, since only overall bank profitability is considered
questionBank.ans: The former are penalised, while the latter are rewarded with rapid promotion
questionBank.exp: Officers who fail the Credit Policy guidelines test are penalised, while officers who consistently get lending right are rewarded with rapid promotion. The other options reverse this, deny any distinction, or drop the stated reward.

questionBank.q: Two junior officers have identical years of service. One has a strong track record of sound lending decisions; the other does not. Based on the stated Career Perspective on credit analysis, which statement follows?
opts: The officer with the strong lending track record is more likely to be promoted ahead of the other
The officer without the strong track record is more likely to be promoted, since risk-taking is rewarded
Both officers are equally likely to be promoted, since tenure is the only factor considered
Neither officer's promotion is affected by their lending track record, only by exam results
questionBank.ans: The officer with the strong lending track record is more likely to be promoted ahead of the other
questionBank.exp: The Career Perspective ties rapid promotion to consistently getting lending right, so the officer with the stronger track record is more likely to be promoted ahead of the other. The other options contradict this by relying on tenure, rewarding poor judgement, or citing a factor not stated.

questionBank.q: A newly disbursed facility begins showing early repayment delays. The account officer's response is to review the file regularly and stay in contact with the borrower, rather than immediately demanding full repayment. Which key success factor is this response most directly an example of, and within which stage of the credit process is it occurring?
opts: Credit Risk Assessment Skills, within Credit Monitoring & Management
Credit Risk Assessment Skills, within Credit Collection
Attention to Detail, within Credit Analysis
Ethical Judgement, within Credit Monitoring & Management
questionBank.ans: Credit Risk Assessment Skills, within Credit Monitoring & Management
questionBank.exp: Responding to early delays by monitoring rather than demanding repayment reflects Credit Risk Assessment Skills, applied during Credit Monitoring & Management — the stage covering potential default. The other options substitute a different factor or place the activity at the wrong stage.

questionBank.q: An analyst handling several loan files at once prioritizes the applications nearest their committee deadline first, so that no file misses its review window. Which other key success factor is being demonstrated?
opts: Ability to propose appropriate credit structure & risk mitigants
questionBank.exp: Prioritizing files by deadline to avoid missed review windows is Time Management. The other factors describe structuring facilities, understanding a customer's business, and weighing risk against reward, none of which describes deadline prioritization.

questionBank.q: Weighing the size of a facility's potential loss against the income it could generate for the bank is described among the analyst's other key success factors as which ability?
opts: Ability to propose appropriate credit structure & risk mitigants
questionBank.exp: Weighing potential loss against potential income is the Ability to match risk & reward. The other factors involve structuring facilities, a fixed profit formula, and knowledge of the customer's business respectively.

questionBank.q: A bank's expectation of a borrower in a lending situation includes all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Timely submission of audited financial statements
questionBank.exp: The bank expects timely repayment of principal AND timely payment of interest. Financial statement submission is a condition/covenant, not a primary expectation (Page 14).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a regulatory reason for bank lending?
opts: To maintain capital and liquidity adequacy
questionBank.ans: To maintain capital and liquidity adequacy
questionBank.exp: Banks are required to maintain a certain level of lending as part of capital and liquidity adequacy requirements (Page 15).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a fundamental issue a credit analyst must address when assessing a loan request?
opts: The borrower's repayment capacity and willingness
The number of branches the bank has
questionBank.ans: The borrower's repayment capacity and willingness
questionBank.exp: Fundamental credit issues revolve around the borrower's ability and willingness to repay (Page 19).

questionBank.q: In the credit cycle, which stage immediately follows 'Credit Analysis'?
questionBank.exp: The sequence is: Credit Marketing → Application Submission → Credit Analysis → Credit Decision Making → Legal & Documentation → Credit Monitoring → Credit Collection (Page 21).

questionBank.q: Which stage of the credit cycle involves reviewing the borrower's financial stability and risk assessment?
questionBank.exp: Credit Analysis is explicitly described as reviewing financial stability and risk assessment (Page 21).

questionBank.q: In credit decision-making, a credit committee can take three possible decisions. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
opts: Automatically approve all loans above a certain limit
Defer the decision pending further information
questionBank.exp: The three decisions are approve, decline, or defer (seek more info) – not automatic approval (Page 24).

questionBank.q: During a marketing call to a prospective borrower, what is the key issue the credit analyst should bear in mind?
opts: The borrower's preferred mode of communication
questionBank.exp: Character and capacity are foundational to credit assessment; other factors are secondary (Page 23).

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the business model of a franchise?
opts: A business that manufactures goods from raw materials
A business that uses a licensed brand and operating system from a parent company
A business that arranges transactions between buyers and sellers
A business that sells products on behalf of other companies
questionBank.ans: A business that uses a licensed brand and operating system from a parent company
questionBank.exp: A franchise operates under a licence from a franchisor, using its brand and system (Page 24).

questionBank.q: Which business model involves acting as an intermediary between buyers and sellers without taking ownership of goods?
questionBank.exp: An agency represents principals and facilitates transactions without taking title to goods (Page 24).

questionBank.q: Why is the credit analyst required to understand a customer's business model before lending?
opts: To calculate the customer's net worth
To determine the customer's personal preferences
To identify the key risks and cash flow drivers of the business
questionBank.ans: To identify the key risks and cash flow drivers of the business
questionBank.exp: Understanding the business model helps identify risks and how cash is generated, which is essential for repayment assessment (Page 24).

questionBank.q: In the credit thought process, which step involves collating necessary information about the borrower?
questionBank.exp: Gathering Information is the step where the analyst collects key documents and data about the borrower (Page 16).

questionBank.q: A bank's decision to lend must consider both the borrower's willingness and ability to repay. Which 'C' of credit primarily addresses willingness?
questionBank.exp: Character reflects integrity and commitment to repay – i.e., willingness (Page 48).

questionBank.q: In the credit cycle, what is the final stage after loan termination?
questionBank.exp: The cycle ends with Loan Termination and then Post-Loan Analysis (Page 22).

questionBank.q: Why is it important for a credit analyst to avoid or disclose personal interest/relationship with a borrower?
opts: To speed up the approval process
questionBank.exp: Disclosing relationships prevents bias and ensures objective credit assessment (Page 44).

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the 'Credit Decision Making' stage?
opts: Deciding whether to lend and structuring the loan terms
Approving the loan without any conditions
Marketing the loan to other banks
questionBank.ans: Deciding whether to lend and structuring the loan terms
questionBank.exp: Credit Decision Making involves the choice to lend or not, and the structuring of the facility (Page 21).

questionBank.q: A borrower who has a high level of integrity and a good track record is said to have strong:
questionBank.exp: Character refers to management's integrity and commitment to repay (Page 48).

questionBank.q: The 'Credit Thought Process' includes a sequential order of steps. Which of the following is the correct order?
opts: Industry Analysis → Financial Analysis → Identification → Gathering Info → Decision
Financial Analysis → Identification → Gathering Info → Industry Analysis → Decision
Gathering Info → Financial Analysis → Identification → Decision → Industry Analysis
Identification → Gathering Info → Financial Analysis → Industry Analysis → Decision
questionBank.ans: Identification → Gathering Info → Financial Analysis → Industry Analysis → Decision
questionBank.exp: The correct order is: Identification, Gathering Information, Financial Analysis, Industry & Market Analysis, then Decision (Page 16-17).

questionBank.q: Why do banks require a certain level of lending as part of their capital and liquidity adequacy requirements?
questionBank.exp: This is a regulatory requirement (Page 15).

questionBank.q: What is the primary source of income for most banks?
questionBank.exp: Lending is the primary and largest source of income for banks (Page 15).

questionBank.q: In the credit cycle, which stage is responsible for ensuring all legal documentation is in place before disbursement?
questionBank.exp: The Legal & Documentation stage ensures proper documentation (Page 21).

questionBank.q: A credit analyst must be able to understand a customer's business model. Which of the following is NOT a business model type mentioned?
questionBank.exp: E-commerce is not listed; the listed types are Franchise, Agency, Manufacturing, Brokers, and Logistics (Page 24).

questionBank.q: Which sequence correctly reflects the top-down approach to macroeconomic analysis?
opts: Global Economic Analysis, Local Economic Analysis, Industry Analysis, Company Analysis
Industry Analysis, Global Economic Analysis, Local Economic Analysis, Company Analysis
Local Economic Analysis, Global Economic Analysis, Company Analysis, Industry Analysis
Company Analysis, Industry Analysis, Local Economic Analysis, Global Economic Analysis
questionBank.ans: Global Economic Analysis, Local Economic Analysis, Industry Analysis, Company Analysis
questionBank.exp: The top-down approach moves from Global Economic Analysis to Local Economic Analysis, then Industry Analysis, then Company Analysis. The other options reorder these levels out of sequence.

questionBank.q: An analyst checks global GDP growth and inflation trends for one part of an assessment, then separately checks how naira-dollar rate swings affect a client's import costs for another part. Which two components of Global Economic Analysis is the analyst using, respectively?
opts: Macroeconomic Indicators, then Global Trade Dynamics
Macroeconomic Indicators, then Currency Exchange Rates
Currency Exchange Rates, then Macroeconomic Indicators
Global Trade Dynamics, then Macroeconomic Indicators
questionBank.ans: Macroeconomic Indicators, then Currency Exchange Rates
questionBank.exp: GDP growth and inflation are Macroeconomic Indicators; exchange-rate impact on costs is the Currency Exchange Rates component. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: An analyst compares urban and rural economic conditions within the same country, noting disparities between industrial and agricultural sectors. Which component of Local Economic Analysis is being applied?
questionBank.exp: Comparing urban vs. rural, or industrial vs. agricultural conditions within one country, is Regional Variances. The other options describe national-level policy factors, international trade, or industry-level performance respectively.

questionBank.q: An analyst reviews a company's revenue, cash flow, and balance sheet strength to gauge its financial health. Which component of Company Analysis is this?
questionBank.exp: Reviewing revenue, cash flow, and balance sheet strength is Financial Performance. The other components involve market share/brand positioning, leadership quality, and industry-level performance respectively.

questionBank.q: By starting with macroeconomic risks and trends, a credit team is able to better judge how those risks might filter down to affect a specific borrower. Separately, the same team uses prevailing economic conditions to decide which sectors it should direct more lending toward. Which reasons for the top-down approach do these two practices respectively illustrate?
questionBank.exp: Judging how macro risks filter down to a borrower is Risk Assessment; directing lending toward favoured sectors based on conditions is Strategic Allocation. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: Nigeria finances a large share of its imports and domestic production using oil export receipts. When the 2008 sub-prime mortgage crisis struck the United States, it went on to affect Nigeria's own capital and money markets. Together, what do these two facts most directly illustrate about Nigeria's economy?
opts: Its dependence on diaspora remittances as the primary channel for external shocks
Its near-total insulation from developments in the global economy
Its reliance on regional West African trade agreements as the main external link
Its strong exposure to developments in the global economy
questionBank.ans: Its strong exposure to developments in the global economy
questionBank.exp: Heavy reliance on oil export receipts and the spillover from a U.S.-based crisis both point to strong exposure to the global economy. The other options assert insulation or name channels not indicated by these two facts.

questionBank.q: A strike halts output at a major refinery, cutting the fuel supply reaching the market. Separately, a one-off cash transfer programme raises household spending nationwide. Which type of shock does each event represent, respectively?
questionBank.exp: A refinery strike cutting output is a supply shock (affecting production capacity); a cash transfer raising spending is a demand shock (affecting demand for goods and services). The other options reverse or misclassify one or both events.

questionBank.q: Monetary policy is specifically described as targeting which three aspects of money?
opts: The supply, demand, and price of foreign currency only
The taxation, spending, and borrowing of government
The interest, inflation, and unemployment rate directly
The cost, quantity, and direction of money
questionBank.ans: The cost, quantity, and direction of money
questionBank.exp: Monetary policy targets the cost, quantity, and direction of money (credit). (B) describes fiscal policy instead, and (C) and (D) name related but distinct economic variables not the stated targets.

questionBank.q: Fiscal policy is defined as which of the following?
opts: Central bank adjustments to the reserve requirement
The government's spending and taxing actions
Tax incentives aimed at improving production and investment
The manipulation of the money supply to influence economic activity
questionBank.ans: The government's spending and taxing actions
questionBank.exp: Fiscal policy is the government's spending and taxing actions. (A) and (D) describe monetary policy tools, and (C) describes supply-side policy instead.

questionBank.q: A government runs a budget deficit, and the resulting increase in demand for goods through higher spending outweighs the reduction in demand caused by taxation. What effect does this have on the economy, according to the material?
opts: It has no net effect, since spending and taxation cancel out by definition
It contracts the economy, since deficits always signal fiscal distress
It stimulates the economy only if matched by an equal increase in the money supply
questionBank.exp: A deficit stimulates the economy because the spending-driven increase in demand exceeds the tax-driven reduction. The other options contradict this net-effect logic or add a condition not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: According to the material, increasing the money supply has which effect?
opts: It lowers interest rates but contracts the economy
It raises interest rates and slows the economy
It lowers interest rates and stimulates the economy
It has no effect on interest rates but stimulates the economy
questionBank.ans: It lowers interest rates and stimulates the economy
questionBank.exp: Increasing the money supply lowers interest rates and stimulates the economy. The other options reverse the interest-rate effect, deny it, or mismatch it with a contraction.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a tool of monetary policy?
questionBank.exp: Open market operations, along with the discount rate and reserve requirements, are listed as monetary policy tools. The other options relate to fiscal policy, supply-side policy, or trade policy instead.

questionBank.q: Compared to fiscal policy, how does monetary policy's effect on the economy typically unfold?
opts: Neither has any measurable effect on economic activity
Monetary policy has a less immediate effect than fiscal policy
Monetary policy has a more immediate effect than fiscal policy
questionBank.ans: Monetary policy has a less immediate effect than fiscal policy
questionBank.exp: Monetary policy is described as having a less immediate effect than fiscal policy. The other options reverse this comparison or deny a meaningful effect for either tool.

questionBank.q: Supply-side policy pursues its goal mainly through which lever, according to the material?
opts: Tax policy aimed at improving incentives to work and invest
questionBank.ans: Tax policy aimed at improving incentives to work and invest
questionBank.exp: Supply-side policy focuses on tax policy — comparing progressive and regressive taxation — to improve incentives to work and invest. The other options describe monetary or fiscal policy tools instead.

questionBank.q: Over time, all economies are described as going through which recurring set of periods?
questionBank.exp: Economies go through periods of expansion, recession, and recovery, with the length of each phase varying over time. The other options use terms not stated in the material for this recurring pattern.

questionBank.q: What does the material say about the relationship between one phase of the business cycle and the phase that follows it?
opts: Each phase begins completely independently of the one before it
Phases always alternate in a fixed, predictable order
The length of each phase is always identical
The seeds of the next phase are usually sown in the preceding phase
questionBank.ans: The seeds of the next phase are usually sown in the preceding phase
questionBank.exp: The material states that the seeds of the next phase are usually sown in the preceding phase. The other options claim independence, fixed ordering, or fixed length, none of which is stated.

questionBank.q: An auto manufacturer's sales swing sharply with the state of the economy, while a pharmaceutical firm's sales barely change regardless of economic conditions. How would these two industries respectively be classified?
questionBank.exp: The auto manufacturer's above-average sensitivity to the economy makes it co-cyclical (high beta); the pharmaceutical firm's low sensitivity makes it non-cyclical (low beta). The other options reverse or misclassify one or both industries.

questionBank.q: A business faces order cancellations and rising inventory, cuts production, and reduces its reliance on bank borrowing in favour of internal financing. Which phase of the economic cycle is this borrower experiencing?
questionBank.exp: Order cancellations, inventory cuts, and reduced reliance on bank borrowing describe Recession-phase borrower behaviour. The other phases involve different borrower patterns, and a supply shock is a distinct concept altogether.

questionBank.q: A company updates its plant and equipment, considers future capital needs, and introduces new products as new ventures appear across the market. Which phase of the economic cycle is this borrower experiencing?
questionBank.exp: Updating plant and equipment and introducing new products as ventures appear describes Recovery and Expansion borrower behaviour. The other phases involve different behaviour patterns, and a demand shock is a distinct concept.

questionBank.q: In one phase, lenders rely more heavily on security and put more effort into loan recovery. In a later phase, loan volumes pick up amid excess bank liquidity, and intense competition pushes some bankers into unsound deals. Which phases does this describe, respectively?
questionBank.exp: Greater reliance on security and recovery effort describes Recession-phase lender behaviour; the liquidity-driven pickup and competitive pressure toward unsound deals describes Recovery and Expansion. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: Orders and prices rise above historic norms, optimism mounts, and a business shows reluctance to use long-term financing, substituting short and intermediate credit instead. Which phase of the economic cycle is this borrower experiencing?
questionBank.exp: Prices rising above historic norms and reluctance to use long-term financing describe Boom-phase borrower behaviour. The other phases involve different behaviour patterns, and a supply shock is a distinct concept.

questionBank.q: While competing lenders grow increasingly generous, lending heavily against rising cash flows during a period of mounting optimism, one lender instead exercises caution and avoids exposure to weakening borrowers. Which phase of the economic cycle does this cautious lender behaviour belong to, according to the material?
questionBank.exp: The material identifies this caution — avoiding exposure to weakening borrowers amid others' euphoria — as wise lender behaviour specifically within the Boom phase, where over-generous lending is otherwise common. The other phases and a demand shock do not match this description.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is one of Porter's Five Forces for analysing industry characteristics?
questionBank.exp: Bargaining power of supplier is one of Porter's Five Forces, alongside threats of substitutes, bargaining power of buyer, rivalry among competitors, and threats of entrants. The other options name groups not part of the framework.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a barrier to entry into an industry?
opts: Large capital requirements or the need to gain economies of scale quickly
questionBank.ans: Large capital requirements or the need to gain economies of scale quickly
questionBank.exp: Large capital requirements, or the need to gain economies of scale quickly, is listed as a barrier to entry. The other options describe the opposite condition of each listed barrier, which would make entry easier rather than harder.

questionBank.q: In one market, a handful of concentrated suppliers control most of the raw material and switching suppliers is costly. In a separate market, a small number of large customers buy in volume and can easily switch to standardized alternatives. Which force is strong in each market, respectively?
opts: Bargaining power of supplier, then bargaining power of buyer
Bargaining power of supplier, then threats of entrants
Bargaining power of buyer, then bargaining power of supplier
Threats of substitutes, then rivalry among competitors
questionBank.ans: Bargaining power of supplier, then bargaining power of buyer
questionBank.exp: Concentrated suppliers with high switching costs describe strong bargaining power of supplier; large-volume customers who can easily switch describe strong bargaining power of buyer. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: The relative price of a substitute product is falling, and customers' switching costs to that substitute are also declining. What does this indicate, according to the material?
opts: The competitive strength of the substitute is rising
questionBank.ans: The competitive strength of the substitute is rising
questionBank.exp: A falling relative price and declining switching costs both raise the competitive strength of the substitute product. The other options describe unrelated forces that this scenario does not directly speak to.

questionBank.q: An industry sees its number of competitors rise while overall demand for its products slows. Following the framework's logic, what does this combination most directly lead to?
opts: No meaningful change to rivalry or profitability, since these are independent factors
Intensifying rivalry, which typically raises industry profits as competitors innovate
Reduced rivalry, since more competitors spreads out customer demand
Intensifying rivalry, which drives industry profits down and can make the industry unattractive
questionBank.ans: Intensifying rivalry, which drives industry profits down and can make the industry unattractive
questionBank.exp: More competitors combined with slowing demand intensifies rivalry, and as rivalry intensifies, industry profits decline — potentially making the industry inherently unattractive. The other options misstate the direction of the profit effect or deny the relationship entirely.

questionBank.q: The Basis for Analyzing Industry Characteristics splits industry-specific risk factors into two broad categories. Which pair correctly names them?
questionBank.exp: Industry-specific risk is analysed through Market factors (size, growth, structure, and similar) and Product factors (differentiation, technological change, and similar). The other pairings substitute categories not used by this framework.

questionBank.q: A manufacturer benefits from years of accumulated production experience that steadily lowers its unit costs relative to newer entrants. Which product-related industry risk factor does this illustrate?
questionBank.exp: Accumulated experience lowering unit costs over time is a Learning effect. The other options describe distinct product-related factors — shifts in technology, differences between products, and the cost of entering or leaving the industry.

questionBank.q: Placed in the correct order, which sequence reflects the stages of the industry life cycle?
questionBank.exp: The industry life cycle runs Start-up, Consolidation, Maturity, then Relative Decline, with sales growth slowing at each successive stage. The other options reorder these stages out of sequence.

questionBank.q: Consulting the industry life-cycle framework, a lending team is deciding between financing a business in a high-growth Start-up industry and one in a slower-growing, more Mature industry. Which of the following reflects the contrarian view attributed to investor Peter Lynch on this choice?
opts: He states a preference for the high-growth industry over the low-growth one
He states a preference for avoiding both types of industry entirely
He states a preference for the low-growth industry over the high-growth one
He states that growth stage should have no bearing on the decision
questionBank.ans: He states a preference for the low-growth industry over the high-growth one
questionBank.exp: Peter Lynch is quoted as preferring to invest in a low-growth industry over a high-growth one with a lot of "sound and fury," a contrarian view against the intuitive assumption that faster growth is always better. The other options misstate or deny his stated preference.

questionBank.q: According to the material, industries can be grouped according to which of the following bases?
opts: Usage of a particular raw material, homogeneity of finished products, or common services
Number of employees relative to industry average
Currency in which the industry primarily transacts
questionBank.ans: Usage of a particular raw material, homogeneity of finished products, or common services
questionBank.exp: Industries can be grouped by usage of a particular raw material (e.g. cocoa industry), homogeneity of finished products (e.g. textile industry), or common services (e.g. banking). The other options name bases not used in the material.

questionBank.q: A single producer controls the entire supply of a market, and a bank is considering a credit relationship with this producer. Based on the material's guidance on monopoly market structure, which additional factor should the bank specifically weigh?
opts: The producer's total headcount across all its regional branches
The price elasticity of demand for the industry's product or service
The number of years since the producer was first incorporated
The average tenure of similar facilities issued elsewhere in the portfolio
questionBank.ans: The price elasticity of demand for the industry's product or service
questionBank.exp: For a monopoly, the material specifically advises considering the price elasticity of demand for the industry's product or service, alongside the generally lower credit risk of dealing with a single dominant producer. The other options are not the factor the material highlights for this structure.

questionBank.q: In one market, two producers compete through action and reaction, with a leader sometimes emerging between them. In another market, a few producers compete more broadly, and the material advises selectively lending to the firms doing well. Which market structures does this describe, respectively?
questionBank.exp: Two producers competing through action and reaction, with a possible leader, describes Duopoly; a few producers where lenders should selectively back the stronger firms describes Oligopoly. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: A market is highly competitive with a high level of product differentiation, and the chance that any individual firm could fail is high. Which approach does the material recommend for choosing which firms in this market to extend credit to?
opts: Avoid the market entirely regardless of the bank's risk criteria
Rely solely on each firm's brand differentiation as the deciding factor
Extend credit broadly across all firms in the market to diversify away the risk
Follow the bank's Risk Acceptance Criteria closely when selecting a firm for a credit relationship
questionBank.ans: Follow the bank's Risk Acceptance Criteria closely when selecting a firm for a credit relationship
questionBank.exp: For a Monopolistic Competitive Market, the material advises following the bank's Risk Acceptance Criteria closely, given the high chance of firm failure in such a highly competitive, highly differentiated market. The other options describe approaches the material does not recommend.

questionBank.q: A cement manufacturer acquires its own limestone quarry to secure a stable supply of raw material. Which type of structural integration does this represent?
questionBank.exp: Acquiring an upstream raw-material source is Backward integration. Forward integration would instead involve moving toward distribution or the end customer, while the other two options name related but distinct concepts.

questionBank.q: An industry's sales growth has slowed from its earlier rapid pace but remains positive, and the market is consolidating around fewer, larger players. Which industry life-cycle stage does this describe?
questionBank.exp: Slowing-but-still-positive growth alongside consolidation among fewer, larger players describes the Consolidation stage. Start-up shows rapid growth, Maturity shows stable growth, and Relative Decline shows minimal or negative growth.

questionBank.q: Which reason for using the top-down approach is described as allowing analysts to understand the broader economic landscape, providing context for industry and company-specific factors?
questionBank.exp: Comprehensive View is the reason describing this broad-landscape context-setting function. The other three reasons involve assessing risk, allocating resources strategically, and understanding how factors interact, respectively.

questionBank.q: A supply shock in Nigeria is often caused by:
opts: Exchange rate volatility and CBN monetary policy
A sudden increase in consumer spending
questionBank.ans: Exchange rate volatility and CBN monetary policy
questionBank.exp: Supply shocks are events that influence production costs or capacity; in Nigeria, exchange rate volatility and monetary policy are key drivers (Page 29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a demand-side policy tool?
questionBank.exp: Fiscal policy (government spending and taxation) is demand-side; the others are supply-side (Page 29).

questionBank.q: What is the effect of increasing the money supply on interest rates?
questionBank.exp: Increasing the money supply lowers interest rates and stimulates the economy (Page 30).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a co-cyclical industry?
questionBank.exp: Automobiles are consumer durables and have high sensitivity to the economic cycle (co-cyclical) – Page 31.

questionBank.q: Non-cyclical industries typically include:
questionBank.exp: Food producers have little sensitivity to the business cycle (Page 31).

questionBank.q: During a recession, borrower behaviour tends to include:
questionBank.exp: Recession is characterised by liquidation, order cancellations, and cost cutting (Page 32).

questionBank.q: According to Michael Porter, an industry's profit potential is largely determined by:
questionBank.exp: Porter states that an industry's profit potential is determined by competitive rivalry (Page 39).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Porter's Five Forces?
questionBank.exp: Government is not one of the five forces; the forces are threats of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, rivalry, threats of entrants, bargaining power of suppliers (Page 38).

questionBank.q: Peter Lynch preferred to invest in low-growth industries because:
opts: There is less sound and fury, and often better opportunities
questionBank.exp: Lynch preferred low-growth industries because they are less noisy and can offer good opportunities (Page 38).

questionBank.q: When preparing an industry report, which of the following should be included?
opts: Forecast on the outlook of the industry
questionBank.ans: Forecast on the outlook of the industry
questionBank.exp: An industry report should include a forecast on the industry's outlook (Page 42).

questionBank.q: The 2025 proposed budget is based on an exchange rate of:
questionBank.exp: The budget document indicates exchange rate of N1,500/$ (Page 36).

questionBank.q: What is the primary risk of a demand shock in Nigeria?
questionBank.exp: Demand shocks affect demand for goods; in Nigeria, exchange rate volatility and monetary policy are key drivers (Page 29).

questionBank.q: In the economic cycle, which phase follows recovery?
questionBank.exp: The sequence is Recession → Recovery → Expansion → Boom (Page 32-33).

questionBank.q: During a boom, corporate liquidity tends to:
questionBank.exp: Corporate liquidity declines during a boom (Page 34).

questionBank.q: Power of suppliers is high when:
opts: The industry is not dependent on raw materials
The cost of switching raw materials is high
questionBank.ans: The cost of switching raw materials is high
questionBank.exp: High switching costs increase supplier power (Page 39).

questionBank.q: Fiscal policy is implemented through:
questionBank.exp: Fiscal policy is the government's spending and taxing actions, typically implemented by the Ministry of Finance (Page 29).

questionBank.q: According to the material, what is the first step towards lending?
opts: Confirm the business is profitable enough to cover bank charges
Disclose any personal interest in the borrower
questionBank.exp: The first step towards lending is to gather information about the borrower. The other actions are also part of preparing to lend, but they are not identified as the first step.

questionBank.q: Success at loan structuring is described as requiring full understanding of which four elements of the borrower?
questionBank.exp: Success at loan structuring entails full understanding of the borrower's Character, Capacity, Business, and Environment. The other options substitute items from the separate C's of Credit list instead.

questionBank.q: A borrower obtains a loan for a stated valid purpose but later shifts the funds to a different use without informing the bank. Which attitude toward bank loans does this reflect?
opts: Insisting that good security matters more than project feasibility
Doctoring financial statements to appear creditworthy
Obtaining a loan for a valid purpose but shifting its use without informing the bank
Having no stable residential or official address
questionBank.ans: Obtaining a loan for a valid purpose but shifting its use without informing the bank
questionBank.exp: This scenario directly matches the listed attitude of obtaining a loan for a valid purpose and shifting its use without informing the bank. The other options describe different listed attitudes, not this one.

questionBank.q: A borrower alters its financial statements so the business appears more creditworthy than it actually is. Which attitude toward bank loans does this reflect?
opts: Giving maximum cooperation before the loan is granted, then becoming evasive
Diverting company funds for personal use
Exploiting a weak judicial system if the loan turns bad
Doctoring financial statements to appear creditworthy
questionBank.ans: Doctoring financial statements to appear creditworthy
questionBank.exp: This scenario directly matches the listed attitude of doctoring financial statements to appear creditworthy. The other options describe different listed attitudes involving fund diversion, pre-approval cooperation, and judicial exploitation.

questionBank.q: Which belief is listed among the attitudes of some Nigerian borrowers regarding what a bank needs to approve a credit?
opts: That a bank's credit policy is irrelevant to approval
That good project feasibility matters more than security
That documentation quality is the only relevant factor
That good security matters more than project feasibility
questionBank.ans: That good security matters more than project feasibility
questionBank.exp: The listed attitude is the belief that what banks need to approve a credit is good security, not project feasibility. The other options reverse this belief or substitute factors not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is one of the seven C's of Credit (Canons of Lending)?
questionBank.exp: Connection is one of the seven C's of Credit, alongside Character, Capacity, Capital, Condition, Cash flow, and Collateral. The other options are drawn from the separate list of C's of Bad Credit.

questionBank.q: Which C of Credit refers to management's integrity, honesty, and commitment to repay the loan?
questionBank.exp: Character refers to management's integrity, honesty, and commitment to repay. The other C's concern repayment ability, invested funds, and business relationships respectively.

questionBank.q: A credit officer examines a borrower's succession planning, control systems, and track record in the industry, in addition to enquiries with existing bankers and suppliers. Which C of Credit is being assessed?
questionBank.exp: Succession planning, control systems, track record, and enquiries with bankers and suppliers are all listed under the assessment of Character. The other C's involve repayment ability, the broader economic environment, and business relationships respectively.

questionBank.q: One C of Credit centers on whether the borrower's overall liquidity position and asset base can support repaying principal, interest, and charges. A separate C of Credit focuses specifically on whether the annual volume of operating cash generated is enough to cover the loan and any unexpected expenses. Which two C's does this respectively describe?
questionBank.exp: The broader liquidity/asset-based repayment ability is Capacity; the specific focus on annual operating cash volume is Cash flow. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: Which C of Credit refers to the money invested in the business by its owner, indicating how much is at risk should the business fail?
questionBank.exp: Capital is the money invested in the business, indicating the owner's risk. The other C's concern repayment ability, cash generation, and pledged assets respectively.

questionBank.q: A lender examines a company's debt-to-equity ratio to understand how much is being asked in loans relative to how much the owners have invested. Which C of Credit is being assessed?
questionBank.exp: Comparing debt to owner-invested equity is the Capital assessment. A high debt-to-equity ratio signals higher financial risk. The other C's concern repayment ability, the broader environment, and pledged assets respectively.

questionBank.q: One assessment asks how much money the owner has personally invested and thus stands to lose if the business fails. A separate assessment asks whether the business can generate enough cash or liquidate short-term assets to meet its debt obligations. Which two C's of Credit does this respectively describe?
questionBank.exp: The owner's invested funds at risk is Capital; the ability to generate cash or liquidate assets to meet obligations is Capacity. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: Which C of Credit covers the purpose for which loan funds will be used, the loan's own terms, and the broader economic and policy environment?
questionBank.exp: Condition covers the purpose of the funds, the loan's terms (amount, rate, tenor, repayment cycle), and the national economy, industry, and government policy environment. The other C's concern repayment ability, business relationships, and invested funds respectively.

questionBank.q: A lender weighs whether a requested facility is proportionate to its stated purpose of financing new inventory, and separately considers how current government policy and the local economic situation might affect the borrower. Which C of Credit is being assessed?
questionBank.exp: Weighing the loan against its stated purpose and the broader economic/policy environment is the Condition assessment. The other C's concern repayment ability, integrity, and pledged assets respectively.

questionBank.q: An officer notices growing optimism about a borrower's industry outlook and feels inclined to let that optimism tip the decision toward approval, even though the underlying figures have not changed. What does the material say about relying on this kind of reasoning?
opts: It should be weighed equally alongside the borrower's Capital position
It is a valid basis for approval, since positive expectations increase repayment likelihood
It is acceptable only for facilities below a certain size
It is speculative and should be avoided
questionBank.ans: It is speculative and should be avoided
questionBank.exp: The material notes that while positive expectations can increase the likelihood of granting a loan, this is speculative and should be avoided. The other options treat this reasoning as an acceptable basis for approval, contrary to the material's caution.

questionBank.q: One assessment focuses on management's integrity, honesty, and commitment to repay. A separate assessment looks at the borrower's business relationships and the caliber of people in the borrower's circle. Which two C's of Credit does this respectively describe?
questionBank.exp: Integrity, honesty, and commitment to repay is Character; business relationships and social circle caliber is Connection. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: The material gives Connection two possible interpretations. What are they?
opts: The borrower's family background, and the borrower's educational qualifications
The borrower's business relationships and industry expertise, and the caliber of people in the borrower's circle
The borrower's collateral quality, and the borrower's tax history
The borrower's credit score, and the borrower's bank balance
questionBank.ans: The borrower's business relationships and industry expertise, and the caliber of people in the borrower's circle
questionBank.exp: Connection can refer either to the borrower's business relationships, industry expertise, and potential for future success, or to the caliber of people in the borrower's circle who enhance reputation or income potential. The other options name factors not given as the two interpretations.

questionBank.q: A borrower is well regarded within an active industry network, and this network is seen as likely to bring future business opportunities. Which C of Credit does this most directly reflect?
questionBank.exp: Business relationships and industry standing tied to future success potential fall under Connection. The other C's concern invested funds, the broader environment, and cash generation respectively.

questionBank.q: Collateral is described as serving which role in a lending transaction?
opts: The primary source of repayment, ahead of cash flow
A substitute for evaluating the borrower's Condition
A replacement for assessing the borrower's Character
An alternative way-out should cash, the primary source of repayment, fail
questionBank.ans: An alternative way-out should cash, the primary source of repayment, fail
questionBank.exp: Collateral serves as the alternative way-out should cash, the primary source of repayment, fail or the borrower be unable to repay on the due date. The other options misstate its role or confuse it with unrelated C's.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the acceptable assets for collateral?
questionBank.exp: Treasury Bills, Placements, and Residential and Landed Property are listed as acceptable collateral assets. The other options are not named among the acceptable assets.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a key factor in evaluating a piece of collateral?
questionBank.exp: Nature, Location, Legal Status, Value, Marketability, and Convertibility are the key factors listed for evaluating collateral. The other options are not among the listed factors.

questionBank.q: A credit officer structures a recommendation so that repayment is expected mainly from the borrower's operating cash, with a pledged asset available only if that cash flow fails to materialize. Which two C's of Credit does this respectively illustrate as primary and fallback source of repayment?
opts: Cash flow as primary, Collateral as fallback
Condition as primary, Character as fallback
Capacity as primary, Condition as fallback
Collateral as primary, Cash flow as fallback
questionBank.ans: Cash flow as primary, Collateral as fallback
questionBank.exp: This matches the material's description of cash as the primary source of repayment, with collateral serving only as the alternative way-out. The other options reverse the roles or substitute unrelated C's.

questionBank.q: How do Financial and Non-Financial covenants respectively differ in their focus, according to the material?
opts: Financial and Non-Financial covenants both focus solely on the borrower's collateral
Financial covenants ensure profit converts into enough cash to meet obligations; Non-Financial covenants protect assets from depletion and ensure timely information
Financial covenants protect assets from depletion; Non-Financial covenants ensure profit converts into cash
Financial covenants concern only interest rates; Non-Financial covenants concern only loan tenor
questionBank.ans: Financial covenants ensure profit converts into enough cash to meet obligations; Non-Financial covenants protect assets from depletion and ensure timely information
questionBank.exp: Financial covenants ensure the borrower's profit converts into enough cash to meet obligations, focusing on cash flow, leverage, liquidity, or net worth; Non-Financial covenants protect the borrower's assets from depletion and ensure timely information. The other options reverse or misstate this distinction.

questionBank.q: A loan agreement includes a clause stating the borrower cannot sell more than 10% of its assets without the bank's prior consent. Which type of covenant is this?
questionBank.exp: This clause protects the borrower's assets from depletion rather than focusing on cash flow, leverage, liquidity, or net worth, making it a Non-Financial covenant. Affirmative and Negative are a separate covenant classification, not the one this example illustrates as intended by the source's framing.

questionBank.q: A loan agreement includes a clause stating that the borrower's leverage must not exceed an agreed level. Which type of covenant is this?
questionBank.exp: A leverage limit is a Financial covenant example, alongside a minimum current asset ratio and minimum sales or net income. The other options name different covenant categories.

questionBank.q: One covenant requires the borrower to submit quarterly financial statements to the bank within 30 days of each quarter's end. A separate covenant prohibits the borrower from taking on additional debt during the facility's tenor. Which two covenant types does this respectively describe?
questionBank.exp: Requiring the submission of information is an Affirmative covenant; prohibiting additional debt is a Negative covenant. The other options reverse the pairing or substitute a different covenant classification.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is one of the C's of Bad Credit?
questionBank.exp: Complacency is one of the five C's of Bad Credit, alongside Carelessness, Poor Communication, Contingencies, and Competition. The other options are drawn from the separate list of C's of Credit or are not listed at all.

questionBank.q: A lender continues extending credit to a long-standing client without further scrutiny, reasoning that because repayment has always gone well in the past, it will continue to do so. Which C of Bad Credit does this reflect?
questionBank.exp: Assuming past good performance guarantees future good performance is Complacency. The other C's of Bad Credit involve documentation lapses, unclear internal communication of credit policy, and mimicking competitors, respectively.

questionBank.q: A bank loosens its own credit standards mainly because rival banks are lending on easier terms, rather than because its own credit policy has changed. Which C of Bad Credit does this reflect?
questionBank.exp: Following competitors' behaviour rather than maintaining the bank's own credit standards is Competition. The other C's of Bad Credit involve downplaying default risk, documentation lapses, and unwarranted assumptions about the future, respectively.

questionBank.q: One lender assumes a facility will keep performing well simply because it always has, without re-examining current conditions. A separate lender approves a facility with incomplete documentation, no current financial information on file, and no protective covenants. Which C's of Bad Credit does this respectively describe?
questionBank.exp: Assuming continued good performance without re-examination is Complacency; incomplete documentation and missing covenants is Carelessness. The other options reverse or mismatch the pairing.

questionBank.q: Lending is classified as unauthorized under which of the following circumstances?
opts: Whenever the facility is secured by collateral rather than cash flow
When an officer grants a loan above their discretionary powers or the credit does not follow due process
Whenever the borrower's account has been open for less than one year
Whenever the loan amount exceeds the borrower's stated annual income
questionBank.ans: When an officer grants a loan above their discretionary powers or the credit does not follow due process
questionBank.exp: Lending is unauthorized when an officer grants a loan above their discretionary powers, or when credit is granted without following due process. The other options describe conditions not tied to the material's definition of unauthorized lending.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an obligor type in the material?
questionBank.exp: Sole proprietorship is one of the listed obligor types, alongside Personal Accounts, Joint Accounts, Partnership, Club and Societies, Limited Liability Companies, and Multinational Corporations. The other options are not among the listed types.

questionBank.q: Two individuals open and operate a single account together, with both named as account holders. Which obligor type does this represent?
questionBank.exp: An account opened and operated jointly by two named individuals is a Joint Account. Partnership refers to a business structure rather than an account arrangement, and the other options describe different obligor types.

questionBank.q: A borrower shows strong Capacity and offers ample Collateral, but the credit officer's enquiries with existing bankers and suppliers raise doubts about the borrower's honesty and commitment to repay. Given the material's description of Character's role among the C's of Credit, how much should these doubts matter to the overall assessment?
opts: They matter significantly, regardless of the strong Capacity and Collateral
They should simply be offset by requiring more Collateral
They can be disregarded entirely, given the strong Capacity and Collateral
They only matter if the Capital position is also weak
questionBank.ans: They matter significantly, regardless of the strong Capacity and Collateral
questionBank.exp: Character is described as reinforcing the other C's toward timely repayment, meaning doubts about it matter significantly even where Capacity and Collateral appear strong. The other options treat Character as dispensable or substitutable, contrary to its described reinforcing role.

questionBank.q: A prospective borrower's own documentation and figures look solid, but a review of the wider industry and government policy environment shows unusual volatility at present. Per the material's treatment of the Condition C of Credit, how should this volatility factor into the evaluation?
opts: It is only relevant if the borrower operates internationally
It can weigh negatively against the evaluation
It should be ignored, since Condition covers only the loan's own terms
It should automatically be offset by extending the loan tenor
questionBank.ans: It can weigh negatively against the evaluation
questionBank.exp: The material states that a volatile or unstable economic situation can negatively impact the evaluation, as part of Condition's broader environmental scope. The other options dismiss this factor or attach conditions not stated in the material.

questionBank.q: One officer approves a facility strictly within their personal discretionary lending limit, following the bank's normal sign-off process. A second officer approves a facility above their own discretionary limit without the required additional sign-off. How would each officer's lending respectively be classified?
questionBank.exp: Lending within discretionary limits and normal process is Authorized; lending above the limit without required sign-off is Unauthorized. The other options reverse or misclassify one or both officers' lending.

questionBank.q: A facility is secured by a pledged asset, but the credit officer's recommendation is based primarily on the borrower's projected operating cash flow, with the pledged asset treated as a fallback only if that cash flow fails to materialize. Does this match the material's intended role for Collateral among the C's of Credit?
opts: Yes, this matches Collateral's intended role as the alternative way-out
No, Collateral should be weighed equally with cash flow as a primary source
No, Collateral should be the primary basis when the pledged asset is highly liquid
Yes, but only for facilities below the bank's standard lending threshold
questionBank.ans: Yes, this matches Collateral's intended role as the alternative way-out
questionBank.exp: This matches the material's description of cash as the primary source of repayment, with collateral serving only as the alternative way-out if that fails. The other options treat collateral as equal to or more important than cash flow, or attach an unstated size condition.

questionBank.q: A single individual owns and runs a business under their own name, bearing full personal responsibility for its debts. Which obligor type does this represent?
questionBank.exp: A business owned and run by a single individual, with full personal responsibility for its debts, is a Sole proprietorship. The other options describe multi-party business structures, incorporated entities, or a different account type.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a common attitude of Nigerian borrowers that poses a risk to banks?
opts: They cooperate fully after the loan is granted
They divert funds from the company for personal uses
questionBank.ans: They divert funds from the company for personal uses
questionBank.exp: Borrowers may divert funds for personal use, making the company an empty shell (Page 46).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a recommended way to prevent borrower deception?
opts: Accepting financial statements at face value
Conducting thorough due diligence and site visits
questionBank.ans: Conducting thorough due diligence and site visits
questionBank.exp: Site visits and due diligence help prevent deception (Page 46).

questionBank.q: Which 'C' of credit refers to the borrower's integrity and commitment to repay?
questionBank.exp: Character is about integrity and willingness to repay (Page 48).

questionBank.q: Which 'C' of credit measures the borrower's ability to generate adequate cash flow?
questionBank.exp: Capacity refers to the ability to generate cash flow to repay (Page 49).

questionBank.q: Which 'C' of credit refers to the borrower's business relationships and industry expertise?
questionBank.exp: Connection refers to business relationships and caliber of people in the borrower's circle (Page 53).

questionBank.q: What is the risk of 'Competition' as a C of bad credit?
opts: Following competitors' behaviour rather than maintaining the bank's own credit standards
questionBank.exp: Competition may lead banks to lower credit standards to match competitors (Page 54).

questionBank.q: Under the 'Capacity' C, the borrower's ability to repay is determined by:
opts: The number of years in business
questionBank.exp: Capacity is about generating sufficient cash flow (Page 49).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of a financial covenant?
opts: The borrower must maintain a current asset ratio not below 1
The borrower must submit quarterly statements
The borrower must have adequate insurance
The borrower must not sell more than 10% of assets without consent
questionBank.ans: The borrower must maintain a current asset ratio not below 1
questionBank.exp: Financial covenants focus on financial ratios like leverage or liquidity (Page 51).

questionBank.q: An affirmative covenant typically requires the borrower to:
opts: Refrain from taking on additional debt
questionBank.exp: Affirmative covenants are positive actions, like maintaining insurance (Page 52).

questionBank.q: Which obligor type is most common among SMEs?
questionBank.exp: Sole proprietorships are common among SMEs (Page 54).

questionBank.q: A partnership's borrowing capacity is limited by:
questionBank.exp: Partnership borrowings are subject to the partnership deed and partner guarantees (Page 54).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an important feature of acceptable collateral?
